title: Socrates in the Athenian Agora: The Art of Critical Questioning and Self-Discovery
summary: Walking barefoot through the marketplace of Athens, Socrates used his famous dialectical method of questioning to expose pretense and ignite genuine self-examination.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 164: நேருவும் “கேள்வி” போலத் தோன்றிய உரையும்
full_text:
In fifth-century BCE Athens, the sun-drenched Agora was the vibrant epicenter of commerce, politics, and civic gossip.

Wandering barefoot through the stalls in a simple woolen cloak, Socrates spent his days doing what he called the 'work of the god': engaging citizens in searching conversations about justice, piety, and virtue.

One morning, Socrates encountered Laches, a distinguished Athenian general renowned for his military valor. Socrates greeted him with disarming humility:
"General, you are a master of warfare. Could you tell me: What is courage?"

Laches smiled with self-assured confidence:
"That is simple, Socrates! If a man is willing to stand his ground in the battle line, look the enemy in the eye, and never run away, that man is courageous."

Socrates scratched his beard thoughtfully:
"A clear answer, General. But consider the cavalry tactics of the Scythians, or our own hoplites at Plataea: Did they not intentionally feign retreat to draw the Persians into an ambush before wheeling around to conquer? Were they cowardly when they fell back?"

Laches hesitated: "No... that too was courage, coupled with strategy."

Socrates probed deeper:
"Then courage is not merely standing in one fixed physical spot. And what of the man who demonstrates endurance against disease, poverty, or the temptations of flattery? Is he not courageous?"

"Certainly, Socrates," Laches conceded.

"Then courage," Socrates concluded gently, "is not physical recklessness or brute obstinacy, but the reasoned knowledge of what is truly to be feared and what is not—the moral steadfastness to uphold the good regardless of danger!"

Laches realized that his initial definition was incomplete. Through questions rather than dogmatic lectures, Socrates helped citizens discover truth for themselves—the foundation of the Socratic Method.
